own_scenes.desc: Teddy Riley, arquitecto del new jack swing (hip hop con pop y R&B), se mudó de Nueva York a Virginia Beach y buscó talento en los concursos de los institutos: Pharrell Williams (entonces Magnum the Verb Lord) y Chad Hugo, los Neptunes, coescribieron «Rump Shaker» de Wreckx-n-Effect y luego «Superthug» de Noreaga. Pharrell estuvo en S.B.I. con DJ Timmy Tim (Timbaland) y Magoo; Timbaland conoció a Missy Elliott y acabaron en Da Bassment Crew de DeVanté Swing (Jodeci), encerrados en un sótano sin radio ni tele: por eso inventaron su propio género. Timbaland triunfó con «Pony» de Ginuwine (1996), el One in a Million de Aaliyah y «Up Jumps da Boogie»; Missy, que prefería escribir para otros, sacó Supa Dupa Fly (1997) y allanó el camino de Nicki Minaj, Lizzo o Megan Thee Stallion. En los 2000 parecía que todos los éxitos de la radio los producía alguien de Virginia: sintetizadores, voces moduladas, samples internacionales para Clipse, Jay-Z, Britney Spears o Justin Timberlake.

La edad de oro y el Latin Quarter

refs.q: They literally created their own genre of music because they just were doing what they thought sounded dope, and fortunately the world did, too.
refs.para: That’s why those records sound the way they do, because they’re not influenced by anything. They literally created their own genre of music because they just were doing what they thought sounded dope, and fortunately the world did, too.
refs.chapter: Cap. 18: The South Got Something to Say

refs.q: We gave hope to a whole state of people.
refs.para: Skillz (artist, Virginia): I believe that we didn’t have a voice for so long, so, when we finally did get to a point where we had one, it couldn’t just be a flash in the pan. We gave hope to a whole state of people. It’s always been an underdog mindset in Virginia, because we got looked over so much. So when it finally happened for us, we knew we had to be loud and bright and different and original in order to stay. And I believe that’s what made us have the type of voice that we have. I truly believe that we just cut from a different cloth down there.
refs.chapter: Cap. 18: The South Got Something to Say

own_scenes.family: Funk de los ochenta: Prince, Rick James, electro
own_scenes.desc: La era del naked funk abarca las cimas de Prince, Michael Jackson y los dos mandatos de Reagan: recortes, desindustrialización, millones de sin techo, la «guerra contra las drogas» en lugar de contra la pobreza y, desde 1982, el crack. La música negra se volvió narcisista y escapista, del «yo primero»; las bandas, demasiado caras para la ciudad. La industria ofrecía estereotipos (banda pop, crooner, banda funk guarra, según Jon Pareles), MTV no ponía vídeos negros hasta Thriller y Jackson y Prince marcaron las cuotas del crossover. En 1975 trece números 1 R&B eran funk; en 1985 diecisiete de veinte eran baladas. Warner echó a Clinton y CBS sepultó «Pumpin’ It Up»; murieron o se convirtieron Hathaway, Joe Tex, Marvin Gaye, Al Green, Larry Graham. Las máquinas sustituyeron vientos, órgano (el Yamaha DX7), batería y bajo: solo sobrevivió la guitarra rítmica sobre el bajo sintetizado y la palmada electrónica. La insinuación dejó paso al sexo explícito sin cerebro («Do Me Baby», «Beep a Freak»), y llegaron el bass de Miami (2 Live Crew), Egyptian Lover, el New Jack Swing de Teddy Riley y la farsa de Milli Vanilli. Los funkers de verdad abandonaron la radio: el underground (hip hop, go-go) llevó el funk adelante.

influences.name: La industria del disco y la muerte del R&B

refs.q: The Reagan presidency relegated black America into a state of perpetual crisis.
refs.para: The Reagan presidency relegated black America into a state of perpetual crisis. People in the inner cities hooked themselves into a syndrome of escapism. By 1982, a denser, much more addictive form of cocaine known as crack began to sweep the streets in major urban centers. What was once a “manageable” habit engaged in by thousands of disillusioned Americans was now a one-way ticket to oblivion, as crack became legendary for its ability to undermine even the strongest of family ties and moral boundaries. The well-grounded black religious themes of salvation and faith that “we shall overcome” were played out by the 1980s, and a new resignation to the realities had set in. Without a voice, without resources, and without support, blacks began to lose hope.
refs.chapter: Cap. 19: Funk in the 1980s: Super Freaks

refs.q: Within ten years The Funk had been removed from black radio.
refs.para: Inevitably, diverse, meaningful music with a groove (The Funk) had the most difficult time reaching the population. Love songs and mindless disco records owned the charts in the 1980s. In 1985, for example, of the twenty No. 1 R&B singles that year, seventeen were love- and romance-oriented songs, two were straight dance hits, and only one was a message song, “We Are the World,” by the collaboration USA for Africa. By contrast, of the forty-two No. 1 R&B singles a decade earlier, in 1975, thirteen were monster funk jams (five would be considered “message” songs, such as “Fight the Power” by the Isley Brothers and “Give the People What They Want” by the O’Jays), seven were disco hits, and the rest were ballads or easy dancing soul grooves. Within ten years The Funk had been removed from black radio.
refs.chapter: Cap. 19: Funk in the 1980s: Super Freaks

refs.q: Piece by piece, aspects of the organically derived funk sound were replicated by machines.
refs.para: As recently as 1979, all of black dance music understood to be funk was derived from the P-Funk aesthetic: hard, polyrhythmic dance grooves; slick, melodic, yet nasty rock-guitar solos; the keyboard synthesizer bass; complex, methodically placed horns; moralistic, gospel-derived vocals; state-of-the-art, far-out synthesizers; and, if possible, far-out concepts. Yet for all too many acts the P-Funk standard was an unreachable one—eventually even for the P-Funk Mob—and a more diluted facsimile of The Funk emerged. Piece by piece, aspects of the organically derived funk sound were replicated by machines. The producer’s medium of disco music and the promoter’s medium of radio access took the black aesthetic out of the hands of artists, and the inevitable remix took more and more individuality out of each record.
refs.chapter: Cap. 19: Funk in the 1980s: Super Freaks

refs.q: It would be the musical underground that would be the driving force of The Funk through the eighties and beyond.
refs.para: In the early eighties, unless you had a sound that imitated the thin, splinking grooves of Prince and his protégés, were as brain-dead as Rick James was by 1984, or as mechanical and lightweight as the New Jack sound, radio success was not an option—so true funkers did the unthinkable: They abandoned radio. As a result, the New York City Hip Hop scene developed a life of its own based on club action, boom box play, and twelve-inch single sales; the Washington, D.C., Go Go sound flourished—at live clubs, rather than through record sales—as did a variety of underground styles, all of which took off without the support of radio airplay. It would be the musical underground that would be the driving force of The Funk through the eighties and beyond.
refs.chapter: Cap. 19: Funk in the 1980s: Super Freaks

podcast.title: Dominance in Early 1990s R&B
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, the R&B genre had evolved, with "new Jack Swing" becoming the prevalent sound. This shift in the musical landscape posed a challenge for artists like David Bowie, whose "Black Tie White Noise" album struggled to find a niche on radio as top 40 stations favored this and other club/alt pop sounds. "R&B was now new Jack Swing, and top 40 radio was playing more club music and alt pop."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Hybrid Genre Definition
podcast.body: New Jack Swing is defined as a genre that hybridized R&B singing with Hip Hop production. It was highly popular and "taking over the charts" in the late 1980s and early 1990s through artists like Bobby Brown and Janet Jackson. "This was at a moment when New Jack Swing, the genre that hybridized R&B singing and Hip Hop production, was taking over the charts, both from male stars like Bobby Brown. And female superstars like Janet Jackson."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: New Jack City Talent Show Reference
podcast.body: A high school talent show where Pezz (then To Each His Own) and Dragonflower performed was named "New Jack City talent show," referencing the movie "New Jack City," which reflected the "New Jack Swing" cultural trend of the time. "This was called New Jack City talent show. New Jack Swing. Yeah, New Jack Swing because that movie, New Jack City just came out at that time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Post-Invasion Synth Pop Model
podcast.body: The rise of New Jack Swing, exemplified by Janet Jackson's 1986 *Control* album, offered a different model of synth-pop that gave synthesizers "more of a groove." This genre contributed to the evolving tastes that brought the second British invasion to a close. "Similarly, the rise of new Jack Swin, pressaged by Janet Jackson's 1986 control album, offered a different model of Synth Pop that gave the synthesizer more of a groove."
